title: Leading Airbnb through Founder Mode and Product Excellence
description: Brian Chesky describes the transition to 'Founder Mode', restructuring Airbnb's product organization, eliminating traditional divisional PM silos, and running an integrated centralized release cycle.
transcript_text:
Lenny: Welcome back to Lenny's Podcast. Today my guest is Brian Chesky, co-founder and CEO of Airbnb. Brian, you recently made waves talking about running a company in 'Founder Mode' rather than traditional professional manager mode. What does that mean in practice at Airbnb?

Brian Chesky: Hey Lenny. When companies scale, the conventional MBA wisdom is to hire experienced divisional managers, tell them what outcome you want, and step back and let them figure it out. We tried that before the pandemic, and what happened was we became siloed, bloated, and lost our product cohesion. We had dozens of sub-teams building fragmented features that didn't fit into a single cohesive story.

Lenny: What changed during the pandemic turnaround?

Brian Chesky: In 2020, our business dropped 80% in eight weeks. We had to simplify. We got rid of the classic divisional business units and reorganized the entire company by function—design, engineering, product marketing, operations. I got back into the details. I started running a weekly product review across the entire company roadmap. People said 'that doesn't scale.' But Apple did it under Steve Jobs, and Walt Disney did it. Great products require a single integrated vision.

Lenny: How did product management change under this model?

Brian Chesky: We combined product management with product marketing. We said a PM cannot just write functional specifications for engineers; they must understand the customer, the market, the distribution, and the messaging. If you cannot explain how a feature will be marketed and launched to millions of people on day one, you shouldn't be building it.

Lenny: And how does your release rhythm work now?

Brian Chesky: We moved from continuous disjointed ship dates to two massive integrated seasonal releases: the Summer Release and the Winter Release. Everything we build must fit into a unified narrative. It forces the whole company—marketing, PR, customer support, legal, engineering—to pull in the exact same direction at the exact same moment.
